messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Minh was a 46-year-old software engineer, a husband, and a father of two, who had served a tour in a conflict zone over a decade ago. The event that fractured his world was a routine patrol that devolved into an ambush. The air had been thick with the smell of diesel and cooking fires, and then the sudden, deafening roar of a motorcycle engine had preceded the explosion that killed two men beside him. He had survived physically, but the memory of that moment was not a narrative he could tell; it was a series of sensory fragments that played in his mind like a film over which he had no control. He could not put what happened into words, but he could hear the shouts and the engine, and he could smell the acrid smoke.

In the years that followed, Minh built a quiet, orderly life, but the past was never far away. The smell of a specific cooking oil from a neighbor’s window could suddenly yank him back to that dusty street, his heart hammering before his conscious mind even registered why. A motorcycle backfiring in the parking lot of his office building would leave him frozen, his hands trembling on his keyboard. He had come to believe that these moments were not just memories but signs that danger was imminent, and he learned to avoid them. He stopped watching war films or even action movies, as the sounds and images felt like a direct assault. He stopped going to the gym because the rhythmic pounding of feet on a treadmill and the clanking of weights felt too much like the chaos of that day, leaving him feeling exposed and vulnerable. He stopped going out socially, telling his wife he was tired, because the world outside felt like a minefield of potential triggers. He was certain that if he did not control his environment, the memories would overwhelm him.

This hypervigilance bled into every corner of his life. Even inside his own home, the place where he should have felt safest, Minh was on guard. He would check the locks three times before bed and felt a spike of alarm at the sound of a car door closing outside. He avoided unfamiliar places, reasoning that he could not assess the danger in a new grocery store or a different restaurant, and he felt an acute, irrational threat from strangers who approached him, even a neighbor asking for the time. He had come to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous, and that only constant scanning could keep him safe. This state of threat, in turn, made him more sensitive to triggers. Walking to his car, he would anticipate the smell of exhaust or the sound of a revving engine, and often he would find them, confirming his fears. The cycle was tightening.

His marital life suffered. His wife, Lin, could not understand why he flinched when she touched him unexpectedly, or why he insisted on sitting with his back to the wall in restaurants. He could not explain that his memories were not just pictures in his head but a lived reality that could be summoned by a scent or a sound. The more he avoided—staying home, refusing to exercise, skipping family gatherings—the more his memories intruded, as if they were filling the silence he created. His avoidance was meant to control the threat, but it only made his world smaller and the threat of his own mind larger. He had stopped going to the park with his children because the smell of cut grass and the distant sound of a scooter were too much.

What finally brought Minh to seek help was a moment in his own living room. His son was watching a cartoon with a loud, repetitive engine sound, and Minh had a flashback so vivid he found himself on the floor, his hands over his ears, shaking. He was terrified of what he might do next time, of the day his vigilance would fail and he would hurt someone he loved or simply collapse entirely. He was afraid of the memories, but more than that, he was afraid of the life he was already losing.
